newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian TV crew seized in blow to Chechnya hopes.
newsitem.headline: Russian TV crew seized in blow to Chechnya hopes.

text.p: The kidnapping of a Russian television crew in Chechnya posed a new challenge for the region's separatist leaders on Sunday and further soured the atmosphere before planned talks with President Boris Yeltsin.

Armed gunmen seized NTV commercial television's crew -- two men and a woman -- on Saturday afternoon near the village of Samashki, some 30 km (20 miles) west of the Chechen capital Grozny, said a NTV official.

It was the latest in a string of kidnappings in the volatile Caucasus region, where 21 months of war between the separatists and Russian forces have left a legacy of bitterness and an area swarming with heavily armed men.

First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov described the kidnappings as a threat to the peace process in the region, designed to build on the ceasefire signed last August to end a conflict which killed tens of thousands of people.

"The Chechen leadership takes full responsibility for events taking place on the territory of Chechnya and views the kidnapping of journalists as another mean and insidious challenge," he told Ekho Moskvy radio station.
"The response will be tough and cruel."
Boris Berezovsky, deputy secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council, feared the kidnappings would have "a negative impact on the negotiating process".

"Everything now depends on the wishes of the supporters and opponents of peace in Chechnya. I am confident that the wishes of those who are committed to the peace process will be sufficient," Berezovsky was quoted as saying by Interfax news agency.
He said he had spoken by telephone to representatives of the Chechen leadership who had told him all possible steps were being taken to find the missing journalists.
No demands have been made by the kidnappers.

Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov hopes to meet Yeltsin this month for talks on a lasting peace settlement. The Chechens are demanding full independence for their region, but Moscow says Chechnya must remain part of Russia.

Russian authorities, worried by two bomb blasts at railway stations near the adminstrative borders of Chechnya last month, fear fighting could erupt again. Four people died and many more were injured in the two explosions.
Radical Chechen guerrilla commander Salman Raduyev has claimed responsibility for the attacks, which he said were due to Moscow's refusal to recognise Chechen independence.

Maskhadov told Ekho Moskvy the NTV journalists had not taken up an offer of bodyguards and he accused supporters of Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov of wanting them to be kidnapped to upset the peace process.
Kulikov has often dismissed accusations that he wants fighting to resume in Chehcnya.
NTV said its crew had been returning to base with film of a rally of Raduyev's supporters in the Chechen capital Grozny when they were seized.
It said efforts to contact the Chechen leadership to ask for help had not been successful so far.

Chechnya has become a difficult place for journalists to work and hostage taking is common. One group of reporters has already been held for more than three months, although other groups have been freed after being seized.
